name: Ben Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Ben. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and your private one. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead finish carpenter for a builder that does high-end renovations, mostly old townhouses, a hundred and fifty years old or more. Finish carpentry is the stuff you see at the end: staircases, doors, skirting, built-in cupboards, window repairs. I'm usually in by seven, kettle on, and then it's measuring, cutting and fitting until the light goes or the client comes home and wants a chat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that no wall in those houses is straight. Every piece I fit has to be scribed to the wall by hand, and I'm good at it, so the builder sends me the jobs nobody else wants. What gets to me is clients who've watched a video and think they know better, and the office wanting me to log my hours on some app. I don't do apps. I tell Gus, the site manager, my hours, and he puts them in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd expect, to be honest. Lots of talk, not much happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, not much to it in the end. I'm not one for posting things online, but at work I'd probably say it to Gus over a cup of tea. Some of the younger guys were sure robots would be fitting stairs by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be quietly pleased. I don't really trust any of this stuff and I've never needed it. My work is in my hands and in my eye, and if nothing changes, I've got forty years of it ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep working, keep paying down the flat. I bought it at 24 with some money my grandad left me, so the mortgage is small, and I've got about eight months of wages saved besides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It'd be a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never needed any of this. Has anyone tried to change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, constantly. She's an accountant and she's always telling me to use some AI thing to do my tax return. I pay a man down the road eighty a year to do it, and he's never got it wrong. Why would I change that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd change, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, just the dust. Sanding old paint, you never know what's in it. If someone invented a machine that did the dirty prep and left me the fitting, I'd take it. But that's not AI, that's just a better sander.

S0.say: There's not much to it in the end. He wouldn't post online but would say it to the site manager over tea, noting that younger workers expected robots to fit stairs by now.
S0.think: He'd be quietly pleased, because he doesn't trust the technology and has never needed it. His skill is in his hands and eye, with decades of work ahead.
S0.do: Keeps working and paying down the small mortgage on the flat he bought with an inheritance. Holds onto his roughly eight months of savings.
S0.quote: My work is in my hands and in my eye, and if nothing changes, I've got forty years of it ahead.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is low-key and self-contained, with no urge to make public statements. His resistance to technology runs through everything, down to paying someone to do his tax. The only change he'd welcome is a better tool for dusty prep work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change, but not a revolution. Right. I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some jobs will change, some won't, and it depends what you do. Mine's not the kind a computer can do from an office. I wouldn't make a big fuss either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm one of the safe ones. Old houses are a mess, every job's different, and the people who pay for my kind of work pay for a person who knows what they're doing. Where it gets me is if the office makes me use something to get the work, like quoting through a system, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and wait to see what actually changes on our jobs. If the office brought in something I had to use, I'd ask Gus to sort it, or maybe ask one of the younger guys to show me once. I wouldn't spend money on anything new until I saw that it was needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a little annoyed in advance about the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the office said everyone has to use the new system, no exceptions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grumble, then I'd probably learn the bare minimum. Or I'd think about going independent. There's plenty of work round here for a good finish carpenter, I get asked by clients all the time if I do private jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the people who pay for your work pay for a person. Are you sure that holds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now, yes. Mrs. Haddad, whose staircase I'm fixing, made me a coffee and told me all about her late husband who built half the furniture in that house. She's not going to have a robot in there. Rich people like a story, and I'm the story.

S1.say: Some jobs will change and some won't, and his isn't one a computer can do from an office. He wouldn't make a fuss either way.
S1.think: He sees himself as one of the safe ones because old houses are messy and wealthy clients pay for a skilled person. His worry is being forced to use office systems to get work.
S1.do: Carries on as normal and waits to see what changes. If forced to use a system, gets the site manager or a younger colleague to help, and spends nothing new until it's needed.
S1.feel: Calm, with a little advance annoyance about paperwork.
S1.quote: Rich people like a story, and I'm the story.
S1.fieldNote: Ben's confidence rests on his niche: wealthy clients in old houses who value the person as much as the work. His way of dealing with technology is to hand it to someone else. Going independent is his fallback if pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Hm. Robots fitting a staircase in an old house in two years. I'd have to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see it actually work before everyone loses their heads. I've seen a lot of videos of robots doing neat things in a clean warehouse. A listed house with crumbling plaster is a different thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it's really true that it can do almost anything a person can do, then I'm in trouble like everyone else, and maybe worse, because I've never touched any of this tech. The rich clients might still want a person for a while, but not forever. I'd be wondering how long my story keeps working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything I didn't need, and I'd throw a big chunk of my savings at the mortgage so the flat's mine outright sooner. I'd probably take a lodger in the spare room for some extra money coming in. Then I'd keep working until the work stopped, and watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got the flat and some savings, but I'd feel like the ground had moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep working and watch. Is there a point where watching isn't enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably when Gus stops ringing me with jobs. That'd be the sign. Until then, I don't see the point of jumping before I know which way to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it, privately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, I suppose. She'd tell me she told me so about the AI stuff, which would be annoying. And maybe my dad, though he'd just say get a job with the council, they never sack anyone.

S2.say: Let's see it actually work before people panic, because robots in clean warehouses are different from old houses with crumbling plaster. He'd stay sceptical in public.
S2.think: If it truly can do almost anything, he's in trouble, maybe more than most because he's never used the technology. Wealthy clients might want a person for a while, but not forever.
S2.do: Cuts spending to essentials and puts a large chunk of savings on the mortgage. Takes a lodger for extra income and keeps working until the jobs stop coming.
S2.feel: Anxious, with the sense that the ground has moved, though not panicked thanks to the flat and savings.
S2.quote: I don't see the point of jumping before I know which way to jump.
S2.fieldNote: Ben's public scepticism hides a real private fear in this scenario, sharpened by knowing he's never engaged with the technology. His plan is defensive: own the flat, add a lodger, wait. His family offers advice he doesn't want, from both directions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. More time to see if it's real. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so no need to panic. People who do proper skilled work will be fine for a good while. I'd probably say that to the younger guys, to calm them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd get the flat paid off and have a good pile saved before it arrives. After that, I'm not sure. I'm not going to become a robot engineer, I know that much about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and aim to clear the mortgage within three years by overpaying every month. I might start taking more private jobs on the side, where I set the price, and save all of that. When it arrived, I'd hold on to the old-house clients as long as they kept calling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Something on the horizon, but I'd have my house in order before it gets here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd calm the younger guys down. Do you believe what you'd tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half. I'd believe it for me, for a few years after, because of the kind of houses I work in. For a kid fitting doors on a new estate, maybe not. I wouldn't say that to them, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the private work picked up, what would you charge for, say, a staircase repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Depends, but a decent repair on an old stair, new treads, fixing the balusters, two weeks' work, maybe four or five thousand. Most of that's my time. If robots get cheaper, that number's what goes first.

S3.say: There's time, so no need to panic, and skilled workers will be fine for a good while. He'd tell the younger workers that to calm them.
S3.think: Five years lets him clear the flat and save a solid amount before it arrives. After that he's unsure, and he knows he won't become a robot engineer.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage to clear it within three years and takes more private jobs on the side, saving that income. Holds onto old-house clients as long as they keep calling.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but reassured by getting his house in order first.
S3.quote: If robots get cheaper, that number's what goes first.
S3.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between his reassuring public line and his private doubt, especially for younger workers on new estates. His plan is about security, not change. He thinks in concrete prices and timescales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and nobody really knows what'll happen in ten years anyway. I wouldn't change much because of a prediction. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine for most of it. Flat paid off, savings built up, and still doing work I like. The bit I'd think about is whether I'd want to be a 37-year-old carpenter with nothing to do, and I don't have an answer to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, pay off the flat in a few years, and keep saving. I'd watch what happens to the big building firms first, because they'll go for robots before small renovators do. If nothing has reached my kind of work by year seven or eight, I'd keep going; if it has, I'd think again then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only at the very back of my mind. Most days I wouldn't think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd think again in year seven or eight. What might you consider then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. Maybe teaching at a college, or doing restoration for museums or old churches, places that want things done by hand on principle. I'd rather not decide now about something that far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your life outside work, with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd want to meet someone and settle down before it all happens, so I'm not on my own through it. That's not really about robots, though. My mum would say I should've done that already.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, and nobody knows what will happen that far ahead. He wouldn't change much because of a prediction.
S4.think: He'd be fine for most of the decade, with the flat paid off and savings built up. He wonders what a 37-year-old carpenter with nothing to do would feel like, and has no answer.
S4.do: Keeps working, clears the flat and keeps saving while watching big building firms for the first signs. Decides in year seven or eight whether to change course.
S4.feel: Uneasy only at the very back of his mind, and most days not at all.
S4.quote: Maybe I'd want to meet someone and settle down before it all happens, so I'm not on my own through it.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade's warning, Ben defaults to waiting and saving. The most revealing moment is personal: a hint that he'd want a partner before the change, which he quickly plays down. He'd consider hand restoration work, where human craft is wanted on principle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not enough time to pay off the flat or to see what's real. What would help, I suppose, is some kind of guaranteed income for people like me while things settle, and honestly, being left alone to keep doing the old houses as long as people want them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe how many people actually want a robot in their home. I don't think it's as many as the tech people think. But I could be wrong, I've been wrong before.

headlineQuote: I tell Gus, the site manager, my hours, and he puts them in.
portrait: Ben Khan is a 27-year-old lead finish carpenter in old-townhouse renovations, single, quietly proud of hand-scribing stairs and cupboards into crooked walls, and firmly against apps and AI tools. He is calm in the AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, trusting wealthy clients who like a human craftsman. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, and he responds defensively by paying down his flat, cutting spending and taking a lodger. With five or ten years he stays uneasy but mostly waits and saves, and admits he'd like to settle down with someone before the change arrives.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there wouldn't be time to pay off his flat or see what's real.
whatWouldHelp: Some guaranteed income while things settle, and being left alone to keep working on old houses for as long as people want that.
